78	
79	\section{Meet Rule}
80	\seclabel{more-specific-rule}
81	
82	If neither the Subtype Rule nor the Incompatibility Rule holds 
83	for a pair of overloaded declarations 
84	then the declarations introduce the possibility of ambiguity.  
85	To avoid this ambiguity, 
86	we require a \emph{disambiguating declaration}:
87	for any possible arguments to which both declarations are applicable, 
88	there must be another more specific declaration that is also applicable.  
89	Thus, 
90	if the functional is called with such arguments, 
91	neither of the pair of declarations is executed 
92	because the disambiguating declaration is also applicable, 
93	and it is more specific than both.
94	
95	\note{What is "an intersection of two declarations"?
96	-- Sukyoung
97	
98	For function declarations we require that the disambiguating
99	declaration be the intersection of the pair of overloaded
100	declarations.}
101	
102	\paragraph{The Meet Rule for Functions:}
103	Suppose that $\f(\Ps)$ and $\f(\Qs)$ are two function
104	declarations in a single scope
105	such that neither $\Ps$ nor $\Qs$ is a subtype of the other and $\Ps$ and
106	$\Qs$ are not incompatible with one another.
107	Let $\mathpzc{S}$ be the set of types that $\Ps$ defines coercions from
108	and $\mathpzc{T}$ be the set of types that $\Qs$ defines coercions from.
109	$\f(\Ps)$ and $\f(\Qs)$ are a valid overloading if
110	there is a declaration $\f(\Ps \inter \Qs)$ in the scope.
111	
112	all of the following hold:
113	\begin{itemize}
114	\item
115	either $\Ps \excludes \Qs$ or there is a declaration $\f(\Ps \inter
116	\Qs)$ in the scope,
117	and
118	\item
119	either $\Ps \morespecific \Qs$ or $\Qs \morespecific \Ps$ or for all
120	$\Ps' \in \mathpzc{S}$ and $\Qs' \in \mathpzc{T}$ one of the two
121	conditions holds:
122	\begin{itemize}
123	\item
124	$\Ps' \excludes \Qs'$, or
125	\item
126	there is a declaration $\f(\Ps' \inter \Qs')$ in the scope.
127	\end{itemize}
128	\end{itemize}
129	
130	Where the Meet Rule for functions asks for a declaration $\f(\Ps \inter \Qs)$ in
131	the scope, it is also satisfied by declarations in the scope whose parameter
132	types are each a subtype of both $\Ps$ and $\Qs$ and together cover
133	$\Ps \inter \Qs$ (\secref{internal-types}): every value of both $\Ps$ and $\Qs$
134	is a value of the parameter type of one of them, for every value a program can
135	make, not only for the values a program does make.
136	Each such declaration is more specific than both $\f(\Ps)$ and $\f(\Qs)$, and
137	at run time it is applicable to every argument whose value its parameter type
138	holds.
139	Every pair of the covering declarations must satisfy the overloading rules in
140	turn, as every pair of the set must.
141	This case does not apply to the condition on the types from which $\Ps$ and
142	$\Qs$ define coercions: covering does not choose between two coercions.
143	\revision{revival-meet}{The Working Draft of February 2011 asked for a
144	declaration on the intersection itself, and the draft note above asked what the
145	intersection of two declarations is.
146	The answer is the one the team's list of proposed features records for two
147	traits with \KWD{comprises} clauses, ``We agreed to revise the Meet rule to
148	address this with the coverage check''.
149	It is an addition to the Meet Rule of the type group's paper of 2011, which asks
150	for a declaration on the meet; the paper of 2019 has no traits with
151	\KWD{comprises} clauses.
152	Where a trait with static parameters stands between two traits with
153	\KWD{comprises} clauses and their listed types, the intersection of the two is
154	not equal to a named type (\secref{internal-types}), and only declarations that
155	together cover it can disambiguate them.
156	The coverage is a judgement of the overloading rules alone: it makes no type a
157	subtype of another (row~492 of the revival's gap ledger).}
158	
159	Recall that $\Ps \inter \Qs$ is the intersection of types $\Ps$ and $\Qs$
160	as defined in \secref{internal-types}.
161	We write $\Ps \inter \Qs$ to denote the intersection of types $\Ps$ and $\Qs$.
162	If for some type $S$ we have $S \Ovrsubtype P$ and $S \Ovrsubtype Q$ then
163	$S \Ovrsubtype (P \intersect Q)$, but it is not necessarily the
164	case that $S = (P \intersect Q)$ since another type may be more
165	specific than both $P$ and $Q$.
166	\label{adv-over-comprises}
167	For example, suppose the following:
168	%trait S comprises {U,V} end
169	%trait T comprises {V,W} end
170	%trait U extends S excludes W end
171	%trait V extends {S,T} end
172	%trait W extends T end
173	%
174	%f(s:S) = 1
175	%f(t:T) = 1
176	%f(v:V) = 1
177	\begin{Fortress}
178	\(\KWD{trait} S \KWD{comprises} \{U,V\} \KWD{end}\)\\
179	\(\KWD{trait} T \KWD{comprises} \{V,W\} \KWD{end}\)\\
180	\(\KWD{trait} U \KWD{extends} S \KWD{excludes} W \KWD{end}\)\\
181	\(\KWD{trait} V \KWD{extends} \{S,T\} \KWD{end}\)\\
182	\(\KWD{trait} W \KWD{extends} T \KWD{end}\)\\[4pt]
183	\(f(s\COLONOP{}S) = 1\)\\
184	\(f(t\COLONOP{}T) = 1\)\\
185	\(f(v\COLONOP{}V) = 1\)
186	\end{Fortress}
187	Because of the \KWD{comprises} clauses of $S$ and $T$ and the \KWD{excludes}
188	clause of $U$, any value of both $S$ and $T$ is a value of
189	$V$.  Thus, $V$ covers $S \inter T$, and the declaration $f(V)$
190	``disambiguates'' $f(S)$ and $f(T)$, i.e., it is applicable to and more
191	specific for any call at run time to which both $f(S)$ and $f(T)$ are
192	applicable.
193	\revision{revival-meet}{The Working Draft of February 2011 concluded that any
194	subtype of both $S$ and $T$ must be a subtype of $V$, so that $V = S \inter T$.
195	That holds of types only while no type stands between $S$ or $T$ and their
196	listed types; a trait with static parameters may (\secref{trait-decls}), and a
197	static call whose argument has such a type has $f(S)$ and $f(T)$ applicable and
198	$f(V)$ not.
199	It runs $f(V)$, and its type is given in
200	\secref{overloading-coercion-resolution}.}
201	
202	The Meet Rule shall not be difficult to obey, especially because
203	the compiler can give useful feedback.  For example:
204	
205	%  foo(x:Number, y:ZZ64) = ...
206	%  foo(x:ZZ64, y:Number) = ...
207	\begin{Fortress}
208	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \VAR{foo}(x\COLONOP\TYP{Number}, y\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}64) = \ldots\)\\
209	\(  \VAR{foo}(x\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}64, y\COLONOP\TYP{Number}) = \ldots\)\-\\\poptabs
210	\end{Fortress}
211	
212	Assuming that \(\hbox{\ZZ64} \prec \hbox{\TYP{Number}}\), the compiler
213	reports that these two declarations are a problem because of ambiguity
214	and suggests that a new declaration for \EXP{\VAR{foo}({\ZZ64},
215	{\ZZ64})} would resolve the ambiguity. As another example, consider:
216	
217	% bar(x:Printable) = ...
218	% bar(x:Throwable) = ...
219	\begin{Fortress}
220	{\tt~}\pushtabs\=\+\( \VAR{bar}(x\COLONOP\TYP{Printable}) = \ldots\)\\
221	\( \VAR{bar}(x\COLONOP\TYP{Throwable}) = \ldots\)\-\\\poptabs
222	\end{Fortress}
223	
224	Assuming that $\hbox{\TYP{Printable}}$ and $\hbox{\TYP{Throwable}}$
225	are neither comparable by the subtyping relation nor disjoint, the
226	compiler reports that these two declarations are a problem because
227	\TYP{Printable} and \TYP{Throwable} are incomparable but possibly
228	overlapping types.
229	As a result, these two declarations are statically rejected.
230	
231	Unlike for functions, the Meet Rule for dotted methods only applies to
232	dotted methods that are provided by the same trait or object.  This is
233	possible because two dotted methods are applicable to a given call
234	$\As_0.f(\As)$ only if they are both provided by the trait or object
235	$\As_0$.
236	
237	\paragraph{The Meet Rule for Dotted Methods:}
238	Suppose that $\Ps_0.\f(\Ps)$ and $\Qs_0.\f(\Qs)$ are two dotted method
239	declarations provided by a trait or object $C$ such that neither
240	$(\Ps_0, \Ps)$ nor $(\Qs_0, \Qs)$ is a subtype of the other and $\Ps$
241	and $\Qs$ are not incompatible with one another.
242	Let $\mathpzc{S}$ be the set of
243	types that $\Ps$ defines coercions from and $\mathpzc{T}$ be the set
244	of types that $\Qs$ defines coercions from.
245	$\Ps_0.\f(\Ps)$ and
246	$\Qs_0.\f(\Qs)$ are a valid overloading if
247	there is a declaration $\Rs_0.\f(\Ps
248	\inter \Qs)$ provided by $C$ with $\Rs_0 \Ovrsubtype (\Ps_0 \inter
249	\Qs_0)$.
250	
251	all of the following hold:
252	\begin{itemize}
253	\item
254	either $\Ps \excludes \Qs$ or there is a declaration $\Rs_0.\f(\Ps
255	\inter \Qs)$ provided by $C$ with $\Rs_0 \Ovrsubtype (\Ps_0 \inter
256	\Qs_0)$, and
257	\item
258	either $\Ps \morespecific \Qs$ or $\Qs \morespecific \Ps$ or
259	for all $\Ps' \in \mathpzc{S}$ and
260	$\Qs' \in \mathpzc{T}$ one of the two conditions holds:
261	\begin{itemize}
262	\item
263	$\Ps' \excludes \Qs'$, or
264	\item
265	there is a declaration $\Rs_0.\f(\Ps' \inter \Qs')$ provided by $C$
266	with $\Rs_0 \Ovrsubtype (\Ps_0 \inter \Qs_0)$.
267	\end{itemize}
268	\end{itemize}
269	
270	Recall that functional methods can be viewed semantically as top-level
271	functions, as described in \secref{methods}.  However, treating
272	functional methods as top-level functions for determining valid
273	overloading is too restrictive.  In the following example:
274	\input{\home/advanced/examples/Overloading.tex}
275	if the functional methods were interpreted as top-level functions then
276	this program would define two top-level functions with parameter types
277	\EXP{\mathbb{Z}} and \EXP{\mathbb{R}}.
278	These declarations would be
279	statically rejected as
280	an invalid overloading because there is no
281	relation between \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} and \EXP{\mathbb{R}}; another trait
282	may extend them both without declaring its own version of the
283	functional method which may lead to an ambiguous call at run time.
284	However, notice that declaraions are ambiguous only for calls on
285	arguments that extend both \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} and \EXP{\mathbb{R}}, and
286	any type that extends both can include a new declaration that
287	disambiguates them.  We use this intuition to allow such overloadings.
288	
289	\paragraph{The Meet Rule for Functional Methods:}
290	Suppose that $\f(\Ps)$ and $\f(\Qs)$ are two functional method
291	declarations occurring in trait or object declarations or object expressions
292	such that neither $\Ps$ nor $\Qs$ is a subtype of the other and $\Ps$ and $\Qs$
293	are not incompatible with one another.  Let $\f(\Ps)$ and $\f(\Qs)$
294	have self parameters at $i$ and $j$ respectively.
295	$\f(\Ps)$ and $\f(\Qs)$ are a valid
296	overloading if all of the following hold:
297	\begin{itemize}
298	\item
299	$i = j$
300	\item if there exists a trait or object $C$
301	that provides both $\f(\Ps)$ and $\f(\Qs)$ then $\Ps \neq \Qs$ and
302	there is a declaration $\f(\Ps \inter \Qs)$ provide by $C$
303	having self parameter at $i$.
304	\end{itemize}
305	
306	Also, let $\mathpzc{S}$ be the set of types that $\Ps$
307	defines coercions from and $\mathpzc{T}$ be the set of types that
308	$\Qs$ defines coercions from.  $\f(\Ps)$ and $\f(\Qs)$ are a valid
309	overloading if all of the following hold:
310	\begin{itemize}
311	\item
312	$i = j$
313	\item
314	either $\Ps \excludes \Qs$ or if there exists a trait or object $C$
315	that provides both $\f(\Ps)$ and $\f(\Qs)$ then $\Ps \neq \Qs$ and
316	there is a declaration $\f(\Ps \inter \Qs)$ provide by $C$, and
317	\item
318	either $\Ps \morespecific \Qs$ or $\Qs \morespecific \Ps$ or
319	for all $\Ps' \in \mathpzc{S}$ and
320	$\Qs' \in \mathpzc{T}$ one of the two conditions holds:
321	\begin{itemize}
322	\item
323	$\Ps' \excludes \Qs'$, or
324	\item
325	there is a declaration $\f(\Ps' \inter \Qs')$ provided by $C$.
326	\end{itemize}
327	\end{itemize}
328	
329	As for functions, where this rule asks for a declaration
330	$\f(\Ps \inter \Qs)$ provided by $C$, it is also satisfied by declarations
331	provided by $C$, having self parameter at $i$, whose parameter types are each a
332	subtype of both $\Ps$ and $\Qs$ and together cover $\Ps \inter \Qs$; the case
333	does not apply to the condition on the types from which $\Ps$ and $\Qs$ define
334	coercions.
335	\revision{revival-meet}{The Working Draft of February 2011 asked here, as for
336	functions, for a declaration on the intersection itself.}
337	
338	Notice that the Meet Rule for functional methods requires the self
339	parameters of two overloaded declarations to be in the same position.
340	This requirement guarantees that no ambiguity is caused by the
341	position of the self parameter.  Two declarations which differ in the
342	position of the self parameter must satisfy either the Subtype Rule or
343	the Incompatibility Rule to be a valid overloading.
344	
345	Functional method declarations can overload with function declaraions.
346	A valid overloading between a functional method declaration and
347	a function declaration is
348	determined by applying the (more restrictive) Meet Rule for functions
349	to both declarations.

== Specification/advanced/overloading.tex:34-180

\section{Principles of Overloading}
\seclabel{principles-overloading}

Fortress allows multiple functional declarations of the same name to
be declared in a single scope.  However, recall from \chapref{names}
the following shadowing rules:
\begin{itemize}
\item
dotted method declarations shadow top-level function declarations with
the same name, and
\item
dotted method declarations provided by a trait or object declaration
or object expression
shadow functional method declarations with the same name that are
provided by a different trait or object declaration
or object expression.
\end{itemize}
Also, note that a trait or object declaration
or object expression must not have a
functional method declaration and a dotted method declaration with the
same name, either directly or by inheritance.
Therefore, top-level functions can overload
with other top-level functions and functional methods, dotted methods with
other dotted methods, and functional methods with other functional methods
and top-level functions.

Overloading functional declarations allows the benefits of polymorphic
declarations.  However, with these benefits comes the potential for
ambiguous calls at run time.  Fortress provides overloading rules for the
\emph{declarations} of functionals to eliminate the \emph{possibility}
of ambiguous calls at run time, whether or not these calls actually
appear in the program.

For each functional application expression, it should be a static error
if there does not exist a statically most applicable declaration for
that expression.
Furthermore, these rules are checked statically.
In fact, the overloading rules
in Fortress allow the compiler to identify the
statically most specific declaration for a particular call.  Therefore
an implementation strategy may be used in which the statically most
specific declaration is identified statically, and the runtime
dispatch mechanism need only consider dispatching among that
declaration plus declarations that are more specific than that
declaration (proof of this is given in \secref{proof-overloading-resolution}).
One case is an exception.
Where the static type of a call's argument stands between a trait with a
\KWD{comprises} clause and its listed types, several declarations applicable to
the static call may each have no other applicable declaration more specific
than them (\secref{more-specific-rule}).
Such a call is not a static error: it dispatches to a declaration no less
specific than each of them, and where they, and every declaration more specific
than them that the call may run, have no static parameters, its type is the
intersection of their return types (\secref{overloading-coercion-resolution}).
\revision{revival-meet}{The Working Draft of February 2011 knew no such call:
it read a \KWD{comprises} clause as saying which types are below a trait, where
\secref{trait-decls} now says which values belong to it, so that a trait with
static parameters may stand unlisted between a trait with a \KWD{comprises}
clause and its listed types.}

This chapter outlines several criteria for valid functional
overloading.  At any given program point, there is a set of overloaded
declarations that are in scope.  Fortress determines whether there is
a possibility for ambiguous calls from this set by comparing
declarations pairwise.  The following three sections each describes a
rule to accept a pair of overloaded functional declarations.  If a
pair of overloaded declarations satisfies any one of the three rules,
it is considered a valid overloading.

The overloading rules given in this chapter are disjoint.  That is, at
most one rule applies to each pair of overloaded declarations.  It is
possible for new rules to be added which allow additional
overloadings.

\label{adv-over-kwd}
Overloaded declarations may have different static parameters, or some of them
may have static parameters and others none (\secref{overloading-terms});
\secref{overloading-static-params} states how the rules of this chapter apply
to declarations with static parameters.  Valid overloadings for
declarations that contain keyword or
varargs parameters are determined
by analyzing the expansion of these declarations as described in
\secref{applicability-with-special-params}.  Therefore, keyword
parameters and varargs parameters are ignored in
the remainder of this chapter, and static parameters are ignored until
\secref{overloading-static-params}.
\revision{revival-overloading}{The Working Draft of February 2011 said here
that overloaded declarations must have static parameters that are identical up
to $\alpha$-equivalence, and ignored static parameters in the remainder of this
chapter.}

An operator method declaration whose name is one of the operator parameters
(described in \secref{opr-ident})
of its enclosing trait or object may be overloaded with other operator
declarations in the same component.  Therefore, such an operator method
declaration must satisfy the overloading rules
with every operator declaration in the same component.



In addition, a functional which takes a single parameter whose type is
a naked type parameter declared with the bound \TYP{Any} written, as
\EXP{T \KWD{extends} \TYP{Any}}, cannot be
overloaded.  This restriction prevents ambiguous overloadings such as
the following:
%makeSet[\T extends Any\](x: T): Set[\T\]
%makeSet[\T extends Any\](x: T, y: T): Set[\T\]
\begin{Fortress}
\(\VAR{makeSet}\llbracket{}T \KWD{extends}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{Any}\rrbracket(x\COLON T)\COLON \TYP{Set}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket\)\\
\(\VAR{makeSet}\llbracket{}T \KWD{extends}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{Any}\rrbracket(x\COLON T, y\COLON T)\COLON \TYP{Set}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket\)
\end{Fortress}
The type parameter of \EXP{\VAR{makeSet}} may be instantiated with
\TYP{(\mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{Z})} or \TYP{\mathbb{Z}}.  If this is the
case then the call \EXP{\VAR{makeSet}(3, 4)}, where 3 and 4 have type
\TYP{\mathbb{Z}}, is ambiguous.
A type parameter declared without an \KWD{extends} clause, whose bound is
\TYP{Any} as well (\secref{type-param}), does not fall under this restriction:
\library\ declare the factory
\EXP{{array}_{1}\llbracket{}T, \KWD{nat}\:s_{0}\rrbracket(v\COLON{}T)}
beside \EXP{{array}_{1}\llbracket{}T, \KWD{nat}\:s_{0}\rrbracket()}.
\revision{revival-bound}{The Working Draft of February 2011 stated this
restriction for a naked type parameter of bound \TYP{Any} while a type parameter
declared without an \KWD{extends} clause was bounded by \TYP{Object}
(\secref{type-param}).
Under the implicit bound \TYP{Any} it would forbid overloading every functional
whose single parameter's type is such a type parameter, the factory above among
them.
The restriction is stated as the compiled type checker applies it, to a bound
written \TYP{Any}; the checker draws no such refusal on \library.}

\secref{subtype-rule} states the \emph{Subtype Rule}, which stipulates
that the parameter type of one declaration be a subtype of the
parameter type of the other.  In this case, there is no possibility of
ambiguous calls, because one declaration is more specific than the
other.  This section also places a restriction on the return types of
the overloaded declarations to ensure that type safety is not
violated.  \secref{incompatibility-rule} defines the \emph{
Incompatibility Rule} that, if satisfied by a pair of declarations,
guarantees that neither declaration is applicable to the same
functional call.  In \secref{more-specific-rule}, the \emph{Meet Rule}
requires the existence of a declaration that is more specific than
both overloaded declarations in the situation that both are applicable
to a given call.

In the remainder of this chapter, we build on the terminology and
notation defined in \chapref{multiple-dispatch}
and \chapref{conversions-coercions}.

== Specification/basic/components/type-inference.tex:12-53

\section{Type Inference for Components}
\seclabel{type-inference-components}

Type inference for Fortress has been described as a procedure performed
over a whole Fortress program in \chapref{type-inference}. In this
section, we explain how this procedure can 
be adapted to perform type inference over a simple program component. 
For a compound component,
concatenate all declarations of all constituents in
the order specified by the constructing \shellcommand{link}
operation.  Constituent compound component declarations are
recursively concatenated.


Type inference over a simple component $C$ is performed by first
expanding $C$ into a self-contained Fortress program, as follows:
\begin{enumerate}
\item All program constructs corresponding to declarations in APIs exported by
$C$ are expanded so that they include all types and static parameters
included in the exported APIs. 
\item All types provided by all declarations in the APIs imported by $C$
are prepended to $C$. Note that these declarations must include
types for all variables, functions, fields, and methods;
otherwise the APIs that declare them are not well-formed.
\item In order for the resulting expanded program to be well-formed, 
we assume that all declarations in these APIs are
expanded into special definitions that include \emph{empty bodies}.
The empty body of such a definition is a conceptual body which
cannot be expressed directly in Fortress programs.
Because declarations in APIs do not have any elided type,
type inference ignores empty bodies.
\end{enumerate}
Once $C$ is expanded, type inference 
is performed over all program constructs that still include elided types.
Empty bodies are ignored.
\revision{revival-paramtype}{The compiled type checker does not yet infer the
type of a parameter that a function declaration leaves out, at top level, in a
trait or object, or local to an expression block: it refuses the component
with the message ``Missing parameter type for'' followed by the parameter's
name.
The inference this paragraph asks for is not yet described
(\chapref{type-inference}).}

# Record lines of rung C of climb batch 11 (rung-checker-overloading), for the gather

## FACTS entry (section "The checker and the one library")

- **The compiled checker reads what a trait or object provides by the traits chapter's inheritance, and checks an overriding declaration's return type against the one it overrides** (`compile-ladder/rung-checker-overloading/REPORT.md`; rows 610, 617, 619, 625, 626, 637 fixed, and under Q4 rows 620 and 621). A type provides its own method declarations and those its immediate supertypes provide, less one that an own declaration with the modifier `override` overrides and one whose parameter types, self apart, an own declaration repeats (`STypesUtil.providedAndOverridden`, `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/useful/STypesUtil.scala:1622-1695`); the overloading and abstract-method checkers read that set, and each such pair has its return types checked, a pair of equal parameter types as an overloaded pair was, a widening override by subtyping. The per-provider cover reads functional methods without self; the restriction on a single parameter of a type parameter bounded by `Any` written reaches a dotted method; renaming an inherited method's static parameters apart renames every own parameter's bounds; the export check skips a private abstract member; the disambiguator refuses an undeclared name applied to static arguments in a `typecase` arm, "Nonesuch is undefined.", on both paths; a local function whose parameter type is left out is refused, "Missing parameter type for i", as at top level (Appendix I, "The type of a parameter that a declaration leaves out"). The code generator still refuses the modifier `override` (row NEW-C-1). Gated by `compiler_tests/OverrideFunctionalMethodWiden`, `OverrideAbstractMethodWiden`, `XXXOverrideInheritedThroughOtherSupertype`, `XXXOverrideReturnTypeNotSubtype`, `FunctionalMethodMeetCoverWithoutSelf`, `XXXOverloadDottedSingleParamBoundAny`, `InheritedAbstractMethodBoundSameName`, `XXXTypecaseUndeclaredType`, `ExportPrivateAbstractMember` and `XXXLocalFunctionUntypedParam` (with `…AndReturn` and `…InLoop`).

The FACTS entry "The compiled checker judges two functional methods by the Meet Rule for Functional Methods, per providing type, …" says that the check "reads every declaration in an api, and in a component those with bodies and every one inherited from an api"; it now reads, of those, the ones the type provides (the entry above).

======
# Decision record: the type of a parameter that a declaration leaves out (rung C of climb batch 11)

The revision this record backs is the box at `Specification/basic/components/type-inference.tex:47-53` and the Appendix I entry "The type of a parameter that a declaration leaves out" (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`, `\seclabel{revival-paramtype}`). It follows the curator's answer to climb batch 11's Q4, way 1 (`explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-11.md`, Q4 and "Answered."; POSITIONS, "The order of the work after batch 10.").

## 1. The changed passage

Original, the Working Draft of February 2011, `Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/components/type-inference.tex:44-46`, unchanged in `Specification/` before this rung:

```latex
Once $C$ is expanded, type inference 
is performed over all program constructs that still include elided types.
Empty bodies are ignored.
```

New text: the paragraph unchanged, followed by the box:

```latex
\revision{revival-paramtype}{The compiled type checker does not yet infer the
type of a parameter that a function declaration leaves out, at top level, in a
trait or object, or local to an expression block: it refuses the component
with the message ``Missing parameter type for'' followed by the parameter's
name.
The inference this paragraph asks for is not yet described
(\chapref{type-inference}).}
```

## 2. The reason

- The paragraph asks for inference over every construct with an elided type, and the inference chapter does not describe it: "the inference over a whole program of the types that declarations elide (\secref{type-inference-components}), are not yet described" (`Specification/basic/inference.tex:23-25`, again at `:261-262`).
- Before this rung the compiled checker refused a top-level function's or a method's untyped parameter, "Missing parameter type for x" (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/staticenv/STypeEnv.scala:199-200` on this rung's tree, `:192-193` on the base; row 405), a departure no passage stated; and it stopped on a local function's, three ways (rows 620 to 622): "Type is not inferred" (`nodes_util/NodeUtil.java:339`), "TryChecker returned an untyped expr" (`scala_src/typechecker/STypeChecker.scala:598-603`), "Result of typechecking still contains intermediate nodes" (`compiler/StaticChecker.java:264-266`).
- Batch 10's rung C left the three stops as expected failures, under its stop "a crash repaired by catching it without the error the text gives" (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-checker-defects/REPORT.md`, section 10, decision 9). Climb batch 11's Q4 put the three ways to the curator; he answered way 1: the refusal at top level, given to the local form, recorded in the S1 form with a callout at this paragraph and an Appendix I entry naming row 405 too.
- The refusal is made where a local function is bound (`STypeEnv.extendWithBindingsFromFnList`, `STypeEnv.scala:69-77`), the file of the top-level refusal, with its message and its form (a thrown `TypeError`), so that it is reached before any stop and a `TryChecker` that meets it gives up as it does on the top-level refusal.
- The box describes the compiled path; the paragraph stays the standard, as the inference it asks for is the repair (Q4's way 2).

## 3. What the box does not say, and why

- A keyword parameter: the compiled path refuses one left untyped, though `Specification/basic/functions.tex:171-172` infers its type from its default expression; the compiled checker reads a typed keyword parameter as a positional one, and walk stops on a call that leaves out its argument. The keyword parameter is not built on either path (row NEW-C-3); the entry's effect names it.
- A function expression's parameter: where the context expects an arrow type the compiled checker takes the parameter's type from it (a probe, `app(fn (x) => x + 1, 4)` against `app(h: ZZ32 -> ZZ32, v: ZZ32)`, prints `5` on the rung's code), so the box names declarations only.

## 4. The way back

- Way 2, inference of the left-out types from the uses of the parameter or from an expected arrow type: the box goes, with the entry's effect; the three refusal tests (`compiler_tests/XXXLocalFunctionUntypedParam`, `…AndReturn`, `…InLoop`) turn red and are promoted to run tests by topic (walk prints `7`, `49` and `6` for their programs).
- Way 3, the stops kept as expected failures: revert the binding check in `STypeEnv.scala` and rekey the three tests on the stops' messages, as batch 10 left them.

## 5. Route C

The same under route C: the question is independent of the exclusion rule.

\note{The following description is too confusing.  Reword it!!!}
If such a field exists, there is no implicit setter for the field.
An explicitly declared setter method must take a single argument---the
value being set---and return \EXP{()}.
A setter method must not throw any checked exception.
Setter names may not overlap ordinary method names.
A setter method must be invoked with the \emph{assignment syntax}:
%expr1.id := expr2
\begin{Fortress}
\({expr}_{1}.\VAR{id} \ASSIGN {expr}_{2}\)
\end{Fortress}


We say that a method declaration \emph{occurs} in a trait declaration.
A trait declaration \emph{declares} a method declaration that occurs
in that trait declaration.
A trait declaration \emph{inherits} method declarations from the
declarations of its immediate supertraits
except those method declarations
that are \emph{overridden} (as described later in this section) or
whose parameter type (not including the type of the self parameter)
is equal to the parameter type of a method declaration
that occurs in the trait declaration.
A trait declaration \emph{provides} the method declarations that it
declares or inherits.




There are two sorts of method declarations:
\emph{dotted method} declarations and
\emph{functional method} declarations.
Syntactically, a dotted method declaration is identical to a function
declaration.
When a method is invoked, a special self parameter is bound to the
object on which it is invoked.



A functional method declaration has a parameter named \KWD{self} at an
arbitrary position in its parameter list.  This parameter is not given a type
and implicitly has the type of the enclosing trait or object.
Semantically, functional method declarations can be viewed as top-level
function declarations.  For example, the following overloaded functional method
\VAR{f} declared within a trait declaration \VAR{A}:
\input{\home/basic/examples/Trait.Method.a.tex}
\input{\home/basic/examples/Trait.Method.b.tex}
may be rewritten as top-level functions as follows:
\input{\home/basic/examples/Trait.Method.c.tex}
\input{\home/basic/examples/Trait.Method.d.tex}
where \VAR{internalF} is a freshly generated name.
Functional method declarations may be overloaded with top-level function
declarations.
An abstract function declaration
(described in \secref{abstractFunctionDeclarations})
can be provided also for overloaded functional method declarations.
See \chapref{multiple-dispatch} for a discussion of overloaded
functionals in Fortress.



When a method declaration includes a body expression, it is called a
\emph{method definition}.
A method declaration that does not have its body expression is referred to
as an \emph{abstract method declaration}.
An abstract method declaration declares an \emph{abstract method};
any object inheriting an abstract method must define a body expression for the
method.  An abstract method declaration may include the modifier \KWD{abstract}.
It may elide parameter names but parameter
types cannot be omitted except for the self parameter.


\note{
Method declarations that are overridden by some declaration are not
accessible.  They are not considered for overloading checks.

Partial overriding of an overloaded functional is allowed
but partial overriding of a functional declaration is not allowed.
}

A method declaration may have the modifier \KWD{override}.
Such a declaration \emph{overrides} any inherited declaration with the same name
and the self parameter (if any) at the same position,
whose parameter type, not counting the type of the self parameter,
is a strict subtype of the overriding declaration's parameter type.
The return type of the overriding declaration must be subtype of
that of the overridden declaration to preserve type safety.
A declaration with the modifier \KWD{override} must override
some inherited declaration.
It is a static error if a declaration with the modifier \KWD{override}
does not override any inherited declaration.

\VAR{reactionSpeed} and \VAR{catalyze}:

=== OverrideFunctionalMethodWiden.test

=== OverrideFunctionalMethodWiden.fss
(* An object's declarations with the modifier override widen the parameter of the methods they override, so the object does not provide the overridden ones (traits.tex, section "Method Declarations"), and the program type checks. *)
component OverrideFunctionalMethodWiden
export Executable

trait A
  f(self, other:ZZ32):String = "f FAIL"
  g(other:ZZ32):String = "g FAIL"
end

object B extends A
  override f(self, other:Number):String = "f PASS"
  override g(other:Number):String = "g PASS"
end

run():() = do
    println(f(B, 17))
    println(B.g(17))
  end

end
=== OverrideAbstractMethodWiden.test

typecheck

(* A declaration with the modifier override that widens the parameter of an inherited abstract method overrides it, in a trait or in an object, so the object neither provides nor implements the abstract method (traits.tex, section "Method Declarations"), and the program type checks. *)
component OverrideAbstractMethodWiden
export Executable

trait A
  f(self, other: ZZ32): String
  g(other: ZZ32): String
end

trait B extends A
  override f(self, other: Number): String = "f PASS"
end

object C extends B
  override g(other: Number): String = "g PASS"
end

run(): () = do
    println(f(C, 17))
    println(C.g(17))
  end

end

(* An object inherits a declaration through a supertype that does not override it, beside the declaration that overrides it in another supertype, so it provides both and, providing none on their meet, is refused, while the supertype that overrides it provides its own alone (traits.tex, section "Method Declarations"; overloading.tex, section "Meet Rule"). *)

#!/bin/bash
# old-fortress.sh <base-build> <private-caches> <fortress arguments>...
#
# Runs the old code, the base's: bin/fortress of the batch's one base build, with FORTRESS_HOME set to the
# base build and FORTRESS_CACHES to a private caches folder. If the folder does not exist yet, it is first
# made as a copy of the base build's default_repository/caches (36 MB, 0.04 s). The paths in those caches
# are the base build's own, so nothing is translated, and no worktree is made.
#
#   old-fortress.sh <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches compile P.fss    the compiled path: compile ...
#   old-fortress.sh <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches run P            ... then run
#   old-fortress.sh <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches P.fss            walk
#
# Every cache a run writes goes to the private folder: every cache directory and the logs are under
# fortress.caches (repository/ProjectProperties.java:283-299), which FORTRESS_CACHES sets, and
# bin/fortress_classpath and bin/run_classpath put FORTRESS_CACHES/bytecode_cache on the class path.
# Under the base build a run reads the build, the library sources and default_repository/configuration, and
# writes nothing that stays: the parser writes its error logs beside each file it parses from source and
# deletes them (compiler/Parser.java:349-367), so a compile of a program that exports Executable creates and
# deletes two empty, gitignored logs beside Library/Executable.fsi. Two runs at once may share those two
# names; that is harmless, because the base's library parses without errors, so both logs stay empty and
# a log removed by the other run reads as empty (Parser.java:373-377). Measured in
# explorations/coordinator/build-cache-exploration.md, section 6.
#
# Keep the private folder and your programs outside the base build (the program's own logs go beside it).
# Refuses (exit 2) a base build that is not built, and a private folder inside the base build.
set -euo pipefail
USAGE='usage: old-fortress.sh <base-build> <private-caches> <fortress arguments>...'
BASE=$(realpath "${1:?$USAGE}")
PRIV_ARG=${2:?$USAGE}
shift 2
[ -x "$BASE/bin/fortress" ] && [ -e "$BASE/ProjectFortress/build/com/sun/fortress/Shell.class" ] \
  && [ -e "$BASE/default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar" ] \
  || { echo "old-fortress: $BASE is not a built tree" >&2 ; exit 2 ; }
PRIV=$(realpath -m "$PRIV_ARG")
case "$PRIV/" in "$BASE"/*) echo "old-fortress: $PRIV is inside the base build $BASE" >&2 ; exit 2 ;; esac
if [ ! -d "$PRIV" ]; then
    mkdir -p "$(dirname "$PRIV")"
    PART="$PRIV.part.$$"
    cp -a "$BASE/default_repository/caches" "$PART"
    mv -T "$PART" "$PRIV" 2>/dev/null || rm -rf "$PART"     # another run made it first: use that one
fi
FORTRESS_HOME="$BASE" FORTRESS_CACHES="$PRIV" exec "$BASE/bin/fortress" "$@"

content.content:
\begin{Fortress}
\(\mathtt{(*}\;\hbox{\rm  Not allowed! \unskip}\;\mathtt{*)}\)\\
\(\VAR{ident}\llbracket{}T \KWD{extends} \TYP{Shape}\rrbracket(x\COLON{}T)\COLON{}T = x\)\\
\(\VAR{ident}(x\COLON \TYP{Round})\COLON \TYP{Round} = x\)
\end{Fortress}
The second declaration is more specific than the first.
For an argument of type \TYP{Circle}, the instance of the first at \TYP{Circle}
is applicable and returns a \TYP{Circle}, but the second, which runs for such an
argument, returns only a \TYP{Round}, and it has no other instance.
The pair is allowed when the second declaration is itself generic:
%ident[\T extends Shape\](x: T): T = x
%ident[\T extends Round\](x: T): T = x
\begin{Fortress}
\(\VAR{ident}\llbracket{}T \KWD{extends} \TYP{Shape}\rrbracket(x\COLON{}T)\COLON{}T = x\)\\
\(\VAR{ident}\llbracket{}T \KWD{extends} \TYP{Round}\rrbracket(x\COLON{}T)\COLON{}T = x\)
\end{Fortress}
Its instance at any type to which it is applicable returns that type.
\revision{revival-overloading}{This section is new.
The Working Draft of February 2011 required overloaded declarations to have
identical static parameters and ignored them.
The rules stated are those of the type group's paper of 2011 (Allen, Hilburn,
Kilpatrick, Luchangco, Ryu, Chase, and Steele, ``Type Checking Modular Multiple
Dispatch with Parametric Polymorphism and Multiple Inheritance'', OOPSLA 2011),
which the compiled type checker applies, with its Return Type Rule checked over
every instance of the less specific declaration; the pair refused above has the
shape of that paper's own example, which the compiled path used to accept and
then fail to verify.
Neither implementation runs the pair allowed above today: the interpreter
refuses it at load, since it asks two declarations with static
parameters for a pair of parameter types that exclude each other (row~159 of the
revival's gap ledger), and the compiled code generator fails on it (row~537).
The compiled implementation adds one restriction that is not a rule of the
language.
When one declaration with static parameters is more specific than another that
declares as many static parameters of its own, the two must declare them of the
same kinds, position by position, and the return type of the more specific one
must be a subtype of the other's when their static parameters are identified
position by position; for its code generator hands the static arguments that a call writes,
by position, to whichever declaration the call dispatches to (row~398 of the
revival's gap ledger).
So it refuses this override, whose return type names its static parameters in
the other order, where \TYP{Pr} is an object with two type parameters:
%trait Maker
%  make[\A, B\](): Pr[\A, B\]
%end
%object M extends Maker
%  make[\A, B\](): Pr[\B, A\] = Pr[\B, A\](1)
%end
\begin{Fortress}
\(\KWD{trait} \TYP{Maker}\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \VAR{make}\llbracket{}A, B\rrbracket()\COLON \TYP{Pr}\llbracket{}A, B\rrbracket\)\-\\\poptabs

--- a/Specification/appendices/changes.tex
+++ b/Specification/appendices/changes.tex
@@ -2807,6 +2807,64 @@ the type mentioned in (or inferred for) that binding.
 \item[Route C] The same under route~C.
 \end{description}
 
+\subsection{The type of a parameter that a declaration leaves out}
+\seclabel{revival-paramtype}
+
+\begin{description}
+\item[Affected section] \secref{type-inference-components}.
+\item[Change] One box after the paragraph of \secref{type-inference-components}
+that says that type inference is performed over all program constructs that
+still include elided types; the paragraph is unchanged.
+The box says that the compiled type checker does not yet infer the type of a
+parameter that a function declaration leaves out, at top level, in a trait or
+object, or local to an expression block, and refuses the component with the
+message ``Missing parameter type for'' followed by the parameter's name; and
+that the inference the paragraph asks for is not yet described.
+\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; it follows the
+revival's decision of 8~October 2026 that a local function whose parameter
+type is left out is refused with a message, as a top-level function is,
+instead of stopping the compiled type checker.
+The inference the paragraph asks for is not described:
+\chapref{type-inference} names the inference over a whole program of the types
+that declarations elide among what it does not yet describe.
+Before this change the compiled type checker refused such a parameter of a
+top-level function or a method with that message, which no passage stated
+(row~405 of the revival's gap ledger), and stopped on such a parameter of a
+local function, with ``Type is not inferred'', ``TryChecker returned an untyped
+expr'' or ``Result of typechecking still contains intermediate nodes'' (rows~620
+to 622).
+A stop of the checker is no answer that the text gives; the refusal names the
+parameter, and departs from the text as the refusal at top level already did.
+Inferring the types, from the uses of the parameter or from an arrow type that
+the context expects, is the repair, which waits until the text describes the
+inference.
+The full reasoning is in
+\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-checker-overloading/decision-record.md}
+in the revival's repository.
+\item[Effect] The compiled path refuses a component that leaves out the type
+of a parameter of a function declaration other than the self parameter of a
+method.
+Among them is a keyword parameter, whose type \secref{function-decls} infers
+from its default expression; the compiled path does not yet read a keyword
+parameter as one, and the interpreter stops on a call that leaves out its
+argument (row~NEW-C-3 of the revival's gap ledger).
+The parameter of a function expression is not affected: where the context
+expects an arrow type, the compiled type checker takes the parameter's type
+from it.
+The interpreter, which has no static types, runs a top-level or local function
+whose parameter type is left out, and stops on a method that leaves it out and
+implements an abstract declaration (row~405).
+\item[Original text] The passage is unchanged:
+\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/components/type-inference.tex},
+lines 44--46:
+\begin{quote}
+Once $C$ is expanded, type inference
+is performed over all program constructs that still include elided types.
+Empty bodies are ignored.
+\end{quote}
+\item[Route C] The same under route~C.
+\end{description}
+
 \subsection{Passages not yet revised}
 \seclabel{revival-notrevised}

--- traits 521-529
A trait declaration \emph{inherits} method declarations from the
declarations of its immediate supertraits
except those method declarations
that are \emph{overridden} (as described later in this section) or
whose parameter type (not including the type of the self parameter)
is equal to the parameter type of a method declaration
that occurs in the trait declaration.
A trait declaration \emph{provides} the method declarations that it
declares or inherits.
--- traits 585-595
A method declaration may have the modifier \KWD{override}.
Such a declaration \emph{overrides} any inherited declaration with the same name
and the self parameter (if any) at the same position,
--- overloading 469-517
\paragraph{The Meet Rule for Functional Methods:}
Suppose that $\f(\Ps)$ and $\f(\Qs)$ are two functional method
declarations occurring in trait or object declarations or object expressions
\revision{revival-meet}{The Working Draft of February 2011 asked here, as for
functions, for a declaration on the intersection itself.}

--- overloading 134-162
In addition, a functional which takes a single parameter whose type is
a naked type parameter declared with the bound \TYP{Any} written, as
\EXP{T \KWD{extends} \TYP{Any}}, cannot be
overloaded.  This restriction prevents ambiguous overloadings such as
them.
The restriction is stated as the compiled type checker applies it, to a bound
written \TYP{Any}; the checker draws no such refusal on \library.}

== explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md:7-27

## The row template

A row is one line of eight cells, `| # | claim | status | class | spec citation | reproducer | found by | notes / workaround |`, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of its topic section, in number order. A pipe inside a cell is written `\|`. (POSITIONS, "The gap ledger's form"; the proposal behind it is `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md`, section 4.)

- **#**: the row's number, the next free one when it is added; never reused, renumbered or given to another row. 148 is vacant.
- **claim**: at most 300 characters, whose first 150 name the defect or the capability: what fails or what holds, and where.
- **status**: exactly one word of seven, with no second status and nothing in brackets:
  - `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`: it works; it ran and its output is recorded.
  - `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`: the specification settles it and the reproducer confirms it. A row with one half fixed stays `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, and its notes say which half is fixed.
  - `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`: the failure reproduces; the mechanisms tried are named and are not exhaustive.
  - `CONTESTED`: unsettled; the notes say why.
  - `RETIRED`: a source's claim falsified here, kept so that it is not derived again.
  - `FIXED`: closed by a landed commit (`ledger.py close`): the claim's first sentence, the test as reproducer, notes `fixed HASH; full text: history, row N`.
  - `DUPLICATE`: a pointer (`ledger.py duplicate`), notes `duplicate of row M; full text: history, row N`.
- **class**: `kind (area)`; `—` only for `POSITIVE-VERIFIED` and `RETIRED`. The kind is one of `implementation gap`, `library gap vs spec`, `library bug`, `design limit`, `deliberate`, `typesetter`, `packaging`; the area one of `parser`, `walk`, `checker`, `codegen`, `runtime`, `library`, `prelude`, `specification`, `tests`, `tools`.
- **spec citation**: the `.tex` file and the section heading in quotes, as `basic/operators/juxtameaning.tex`, "Juxtaposition"; a line number only against `Specification-1.0-frozen/`; `silent` where the specification does not say.
- **reproducer**: one test (its name, or its path under the test folders; an `XXX` test while it is an expected failure) or one probe path from the repository root, at most 200 characters; `none` when nothing in the tree reproduces it, with the command and its output, or the probe's old path, in the notes.
- **found by**: the stream that found it (`climb batch 8 rung I`, `run-c3`, `apl rung 2`), at most 60 characters; no date and no role.
- **notes / workaround**: at most 700 characters: `siblings: N, M` first if there are any; the mechanism, with file:line and the commit it was true at; the workaround; for a closed row, `fixed HASH`.

A path under `explorations/` that is no longer in the tree is read from history: `git show $(git log -1 --diff-filter=D --format=%h -- PATH)^:PATH`.

content.content: - **The compiled checker reads what a trait or object provides by the traits chapter's inheritance, and checks an overriding declaration's return type against the one it overrides** (`compile-ladder/rung-checker-overloading/REPORT.md`; rows 610, 617, 619, 625, 626, 637 fixed, and under Q4 rows 620 and 621). A type provides its own method declarations and those its immediate supertypes provide, less one that an own declaration with the modifier `override` overrides and one whose parameter types, self apart, an own declaration repeats (`STypesUtil.providedAndOverridden`, `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/useful/STypesUtil.scala:1622-1695`); the overloading and abstract-method checkers read that set, and each such pair has its return types checked, a pair of equal parameter types as an overloaded pair was, a widening override by subtyping. The per-provider cover reads functional methods without self; the restriction on a single parameter of a type parameter bounded by `Any` written reaches a dotted method; renaming an inherited method's static parameters apart renames every own parameter's bounds; the export check skips a private abstract member; the disambiguator refuses an undeclared name applied to static arguments in a `typecase` arm, "Nonesuch is undefined.", on both paths; a local function whose parameter type is left out is refused, "Missing parameter type for i", as at top level (Appendix I, "The type of a parameter that a declaration leaves out"). The code generator still refuses the modifier `override` (row NEW-C-1). Gated by `compiler_tests/OverrideFunctionalMethodWiden`, `OverrideAbstractMethodWiden`, `XXXOverrideInheritedThroughOtherSupertype`, `XXXOverrideReturnTypeNotSubtype`, `FunctionalMethodMeetCoverWithoutSelf`, `XXXOverloadDottedSingleParamBoundAny`, `InheritedAbstractMethodBoundSameName`, `XXXTypecaseUndeclaredType`, `ExportPrivateAbstractMember` and `XXXLocalFunctionUntypedParam` (with `…AndReturn` and `…InLoop`).

  - New row NEW-C-4: an override that overrides nothing is accepted on both paths.

fixes.finding: checkOverridingReturnType (ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/OverloadingChecker.scala:676-680 at 307c1ab69) checks a widening override with static parameters only by satisfiesPositionalRule. That rule returns true when the two declarations declare unequal numbers of their own static parameters (OverloadingOracle.scala:164). So `override f(x: Any): ZZ32` over `f[\T\](x: T): T`, and `override g[\T\](x: T): String` over `g(x: ZZ32): ZZ32`, type checked, where the base refused both. The return type is now checked at every instance (oracle.sa.subtypeUA over the arrows without self), and the positional restriction is kept.
fixes.settledBy: Specification/basic/traits.tex:590-591: 'The return type of the overriding declaration must be subtype of that of the overridden declaration to preserve type safety.'
